title: Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists
summary: The Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) was a significant Ukrainian nationalist group founded on February 2, 1929, in Vienna, which played a crucial role in the political landscape of [[ukraine|Ukraine]] during the interwar period and World War II. The OUN aimed to establish an ethnically homogeneous Ukrainian state through radical nationalist ideologies and violent tactics.

sections.heading: Foundation and Ideology
paragraphs: The Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN; [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]]: Організація українських націоналістів) was established on February 2, 1929, in Vienna, merging the Ukrainian Military Organization with various radical nationalist youth groups. The OUN became one of the largest far-right organizations [[coal-in-ukraine|in Ukraine]] during the interwar period, particularly active before, during, and after World War II.

OUN's ideology has been characterized by scholars as a form of Ukrainian fascism or integral nationalism, influenced by figures such as Dmytro Dontsov, as well as Italian and German fascism. The organization pursued a strategy of violence, terrorism, and assassinations to create a totalitarian [[ukrainian-state|Ukrainian state]].

sections.heading: World War II and Internal Division
paragraphs: In 1940, the OUN split into two factions: the more moderate OUN-M led by Andriy Melnyk and the radical OUN-B led by [[stepan-bandera|Stepan Bandera]]. On June 30, 1941, OUN-B declared an independent Ukrainian state in [[lviv|Lviv]], shortly after the city came under Nazi control. This declaration led to a temporary alliance with Germany, which was viewed as liberating [[ukrainians|Ukrainians]] from Soviet oppression.

The OUN-B's actions included participation in the Lviv pogroms and involvement in [[the-holocaust-in-ukraine|the Holocaust in Ukraine]] and Poland. In October 1942, OUN-B established the [[ukrainian-insurgent-army|Ukrainian Insurgent Army]] (UPA), which conducted violent campaigns against Polish populations in [[volhynia|Volhynia]] and [[eastern-galicia|Eastern Galicia]] between 1943 and 1944.

sections.heading: Post-War Activities and Cold War Era
paragraphs: As World War II concluded and Nazi Germany faced defeat, OUN-B attempted to reframe its political stance, adopting democratic rhetoric. After the war, the UPA engaged in conflict against Soviet and Polish forces. The Polish government, through [[operation-vistula|Operation Vistula]] in 1947, deported 140,000 Ukrainians, while Soviet forces targeted UPA members and supporters.

During the Cold War, the OUN received covert support from Western intelligence agencies, including the CIA. In the mid-1950s, the OUN-B experienced another split, leading to the establishment of the Congress of Ukrainian Nationalists party and the OUN-M transitioning into a non-governmental organization.

sections.heading: Historical Context and Impact
paragraphs: The OUN emerged in the context of the Second Polish Republic's control over [[western-ukraine|western Ukraine]] after World War I, which fueled the desire for Ukrainian independence. The organization conducted numerous violent actions against Polish officials and sought to establish a Ukrainian state free from both Polish and Soviet influence.

By the onset of World War II, the OUN had approximately 20,000 active members and a larger base of sympathizers, reflecting a radicalized youth disillusioned with traditional political avenues. The group's legacy remains complex, characterized by its nationalist fervor and controversial methods.
